title: La Mer, mvt 1 (De l'aube à midi sur la mer)
source_citations: Simon Trezise, Debussy: La Mer (Cambridge Music Handbooks, 1994)
Richard Parks, The Music of Claude Debussy (1989)
Jonathan Dunsby, 'The Formal Repeat' (Debussy/La Mer analysis)

key_plan.role: Très lent — modal/pentatonic introduction (B minor / D-modal collections), oceanic timbral exploration with no firm tonic
Allegro plus animé; principal theme presented in fragments, harmonically mobile through whole-tone and pentatonic regions
Central section: Db major established as the work's home key, supported by long pedals and pentatonic theme statements
Modulating section building to the movement's climax — whole-tone collections prominent
Movement-ending: full orchestra in Db major chord-cluster sonority — 'midi sur la mer' (noon over the sea)

notable_cadences.basis: End of introduction; preparatory dominant function (loose Db V function via Ab pedal)
Cadence closing the central Db section — modal-tonal cadence rather than functional V-I
Movement-final Db major cadence; sonorous rather than dramatic resolution

characteristic_features: Tonal-modal-pentatonic-whole-tone synthesis characteristic of Debussy's mature style
Db major is the work's home key but is approached and left modally, not functionally — V-I dominant-tonic motion is rare
Heavy use of pedal points; thematic statements often float over unchanging bass
Form is loosely sonata-like (introduction–exposition–development–climax–arrival) but resists tonal-form labels
common_omr_pitfalls: Wide-range orchestral score with frequent timbral doublings — voice assignment is genuinely ambiguous even to humans
Frequent accidentals (whole-tone collections, modal inflections) make key-signature-based pitch inference unreliable
Long sustained notes (whole, double-whole) with cross-staff beaming — OMR may fragment these
Tied notes across measure boundaries are common — OMR often double-stops them
_notes: Curated 2026-05-24. Debussy's harmonic language predates tonal-function analysis — 'key' fields in this entry mark modal/pentatonic centers rather than functional tonics. Cross-check is least effective on Debussy because maestroAnalyst's Krumhansl-style key detection is tuned for functional tonality; 'various' is used liberally. Section boundaries follow Trezise (1994). Useful primarily as a regression baseline (catching gross misreads) rather than for fine-grained harmonic verification.
